label: Diffusion models work by literally removing noise from real images
description:
A natural simplification: diffusion takes an image, adds noise, then learns to undo that noise. So the trained model is a 'noise remover'.

This captures the training objective but misses what's happening at inference time.

**At training time**: the network learns to predict the noise that was added to a known clean image. The training data is `(noisy_x_t, t) → ε`. Yes, this is a noise removal objective.

**At inference time** (sampling): you start from **pure random noise** — no real image underneath. The same network is iteratively applied to gradually 'denoise', but it's not removing noise from anything specific. It's hallucinating a coherent image that's plausible under the training distribution.

The more accurate framing: the model learns a **score function** `∇_x log p(x)` — the gradient of log-probability of the data distribution. At each step, the score points toward higher-probability regions. Following the score (with appropriate step sizes and noise injection) walks from the unconditional Gaussian prior toward the data manifold.

This is why **diffusion is generative**, not just denoising:
- A pure denoiser trained on `(noisy, clean)` pairs would only know how to handle noisy versions of training images. Given pure noise unrelated to any training image, it'd fail.
- A diffusion model has learned the score everywhere in the noise-corrupted space, including pure noise. From pure noise, gradient ascent on the score (with noise injection) converges to data-distribution samples.

The distinction matters because it explains:
- Why diffusion generates **novel** images, not just memorized ones.
- Why diffusion can do **conditional generation** (text-to-image): the score is conditional on text features.
- Why **classifier-free guidance** works: it amplifies the score's conditional component.

For a clearer mental model: diffusion is **iteratively-refined sampling from a learned data distribution**, not 'noise removal applied many times'.
probeQuestions: If diffusion is 'noise removal', why can it generate images from random noise that don't correspond to any training image?
What does the score function ∇log p(x) mean, and why is it more accurate than 'noise predictor'?
correctionPromptTemplate: The learner thinks diffusion is just iterative denoising. Walk through: training objective IS denoising; inference uses the same network as a score estimator + Langevin-like sampling. The model has learned ∇log p(x), not just a denoiser. From pure noise, score-following converges to data samples. Ask first — 'if you only fed the model noise that wasn't a corrupted training image, what would you expect to happen?'
